title: The King Who Wrestled His Own Herald
summary: A reunifying ruler stages combat as public legitimacy while mobile raiders and an exclusive resin concession expose the difference between spectacle and control.
source_notes: Reunification after a period of competing dynasties becomes a coastal king whose changed title announces a political achievement.
Consolidation of regional wrestling promotion and a promoter’s performed villainy become royal exhibitions and control of local fairs.
Rapid movement along difficult terrain and ineffective bridge demolition become handcart raiders using paths their opponents failed to understand.
An exclusive resource concession and later struggle over control become resin gathering; fossil fuels and industrial extraction are excluded.

entries.title: Varn of the Joined Shores
entries.body:
Varn’s new title celebrated reunification while omitting the fishing villages that negotiated surrender independently. Their landing rights remained distinct. Descendants seek acknowledgment of that difference without denying that the king reduced raids and restored several useful crossings.

Later accounts make Varn of the Joined Shores the explanation for an entire local change. The surviving record instead places this life among dependencies: an introduction supplied by another household, materials purchased on credit, and testimony given by people with reasons of their own. A biography that removes those dependencies becomes a useful legend and a poor guide to what happened. Descendants inherit evidence and expectations, rather than the ability to repeat an ancestor’s achievement. The practical question is which part of the achievement can be maintained by ordinary people after the celebrated individual is gone.

This belongs to The King Who Wrestled His Own Herald. King Varn reunited coastal districts after rival graves were desecrated in 423. He celebrated unity through wrestling exhibitions, casting his own herald as a rebellious villain whom the king repeatedly defeated. A promoter absorbed smaller fairs and controlled which local champions could appear. The court also granted an overseas house exclusive rights to gather waterproofing resin from royal forests. When raiders advanced along narrow tracks using light handcarts, defenders burned bridges but overlooked the paths known to resin workers. The royal spectacle continued while ordinary coastal households lost shelter. Present custodians preserve both unity’s genuine benefits and the neglected dependencies that made its claims vulnerable.

In the connected record, [The Herald’s Wrestling Yard](b011-the-herald-s-wrestling-yard.md) preserves another part of this history. The terms recorded under [The Concession’s Boat Purpose](b011-the-concession-s-boat-purpose.md) delimit the local obligation; they do not grant a ruler unlimited command over the dead. The unresolved issue in 1248 is concrete: whether forest households can renegotiate the resin concession without forfeiting the boat repairs their coast still needs.

Boats make neighboring settlements accessible when inland tracks become mud. Smokehouses, net yards, and communal ovens provide the places where people exchange reliable news. The dead are remembered through finite promises attached to landing water and particular working seasons. entries.title: The Herald’s Wrestling Yard
entries.body:
A raised wooden yard hosted staged defeats of the royal herald. Workers knew which falls were rehearsed, but visiting envoys treated them as proof of vigor. Its surviving beams came from dismantled shelters whose occupants never received the promised replacements.

The site has changed use more than once. Its surviving structures should not be read as a single intact design: one household repairs what another abandoned, and a later occupant can preserve a wall while giving its opening a different purpose. Visitors who search only for the original foundation overlook the people paying for the present roof. Custody depends on continuing access and maintenance, not merely on a persuasive genealogy. Removing an interesting object may erase evidence of a repair that explains why the place remains habitable at all.

entries.title: The Joined Fair Circuit
entries.body:
The circuit paid skilled wrestlers reliably but barred them from independent village fairs. Smaller settlements lost both performers and toll income. Current members want touring cooperation without the inherited exclusivity that turned a useful network into control over local celebration.

The institution’s public account emphasizes its founding purpose, while daily accounts reveal exceptions, unpaid work, and compromises with neighbors. Membership does not imply agreement. A clerk, a patron, and a laborer can defend the same arrangement for incompatible reasons. Its authority is strongest where it provides something people actually need and weakest where it claims that need as proof of permanent jurisdiction. Reform requires deciding who will perform the useful work afterward. Simply abolishing the name may leave the obligation in the hands of less accountable successors.

entries.title: The Bridge Burning Retreat
entries.body:
Defenders destroyed broad crossings while raiders followed narrow gathering paths. Resin workers warned the court, but their testimony lacked household seals. The campaign’s defeat began with an exclusion of knowledge before it became a failure of tactics.

The event survives through records made for different purposes. A household remembers hunger; a court records jurisdiction; a custodian records the interruption of an observance. Their dates can be reconciled without making their explanations identical. Later commemorations often select a decisive moment because a ceremony needs a beginning and an end. The consequences were less orderly, traveling through marriages, prices, and people who moved away. An honest account follows those consequences far enough to distinguish a temporary outcome from an agreement that still constrains the present.

entries.title: The Villain Herald’s Belt
entries.body:
The belt has hidden handholds allowing safe theatrical throws. Patrons once cited its wear as evidence of the herald’s repeated humiliation. Inspecting its construction reveals collaboration, making the supposed enemy an essential partner in the ruler’s public image.

Material inspection places limits on the object’s legend. Repairs, wear, and changes in custody can establish that it was used repeatedly without proving every story attached to it. Its value is relational: somebody can authenticate it, somebody needs it for an observance, and somebody may suffer if it is removed. An expensive replacement would not automatically inherit those relations. Custodians therefore record loans and repairs as carefully as ceremonial appearances. A collector who purchases the object but ignores its attached undertaking may own something that cannot safely be taken home.

entries.title: The Agreed Fall
entries.body:
Wrestlers announce one rehearsed fall before competing seriously, letting audiences distinguish demonstration from contest. Sponsors dislike the admission. Teachers argue that honest spectacle can be impressive without training spectators to confuse staged certainty with political truth.

The custom is learned through participation rather than a single authoritative text. Households disagree about details while recognizing enough shared actions to cooperate. That flexibility can admit newcomers or allow influential families to redefine the practice in their own favor. Describing it as ancient settles neither possibility. Its practical test is whether a participant can question a demand without losing access to food, water, or witnesses. Local reformers seek finite observances whose costs can be recorded, so that reverence for predecessors does not become an unanswerable demand upon children.

entries.title: The Forest’s Exclusive Grant
entries.body:
The grant permits resin gathering for boat maintenance but specifies no household ownership. Later copies add restrictions on movement. Comparing them could release workers while preserving a legitimate supply agreement, upsetting patrons who describe either outcome as destruction of tradition.

Copies disagree in ways that matter. A shortened phrase can remove a condition, and a copied date can imply that a later amendment belonged to the original undertaking. Dry writing preserves evidence but cannot make an oath binding by itself. Readers must distinguish a record of consent from a writer’s assertion that consent occurred. Marginal notes are sometimes the only surviving testimony of people excluded from the formal version. Establishing a trustworthy reading therefore depends on comparing custody, material, and ordinary expenses, as well as elegant arguments about wording.

entries.title: The Resin Bark Lizard
entries.body:
Small lizards shelter beneath loosened bark and control insects damaging resin trees. Excessive harvesting destroys their refuges. Gatherers petition for resting groves, while concession officers count every uncut tree as lost income rather than a condition of future supply.

Reports describe a living creature before they describe a supernatural emblem. It needs food, shelter, and a place to breed, and it reacts to disturbances that witnesses may misunderstand. A keeper who recognizes those needs can often prevent the encounter later remembered as a curse. The animal cannot be made into an obedient instrument of ancestral power. Where an undertaking changes its habitat, the effect is indirect and costly to other inhabitants. Stories that treat its behavior as a moral verdict obscure both ordinary suffering and the human decisions that altered the site.

entries.title: The Narrow Cart March
entries.body:
Handcarts followed dry root ridges between flooded ground. Their crews traveled fast only because local households supplied food. Military anniversaries display empty carts, omitting the provisioning that turned lightweight equipment into a useful advantage.

A route is an agreement between people maintaining its difficult portions, as much as a line across terrain. Tolls buy repairs only when their recipients are accountable for the work. A passage described as open may still be unusable for children, loaded animals, or travelers without an accepted witness. Seasonal detours preserve movement while distributing its costs to other households. Pilots and guides keep alternative accounts of distance because time, provisions, and exposure matter more than ceremonial measures. Closing one stretch can therefore revise obligations far beyond its immediate neighborhood.

entries.title: The Concession’s Boat Purpose
entries.body:
The clause bounds resin extraction to named boat maintenance. Forest households invoke it against ceremonial exports. Merchants answer that sales finance repairs, requiring a public account of actual boats served rather than a general assertion that every shipment helps the coast.

The rule’s force depends on a stated scope. It governs named acts and claimants, rather than every future disagreement that resembles its original case. Courts have nevertheless tried to extend it, usually when a narrow precedent would benefit a powerful applicant. Opponents do not have to deny ancestor law to challenge that extension. They can ask which promise was actually made, who witnessed it, and whether the required observance remains possible. The difference between a valid undertaking and a convenient assertion of authority is central to the current dispute.

entries.title: The Title Change Feast
entries.body:
The unity feast supplied meat to nobles and fish scraps to displaced families. Both appear under one enormous provisioning total. Disaggregating the account changes what the celebrated generosity means without denying that many hungry guests received a meal.

The event survives through records made for different purposes. A household remembers hunger; a court records jurisdiction; a custodian records the interruption of an observance. Their dates can be reconciled without making their explanations identical. Later commemorations often select a decisive moment because a ceremony needs a beginning and an end. The consequences were less orderly, traveling through marriages, prices, and people who moved away. An honest account follows those consequences far enough to distinguish a temporary outcome from an agreement that still constrains the present.

entries.title: The Resin Handcart Axle
entries.body:
Its wooden axle was replaced repeatedly, allowing repairs on the march. A museum patron wants a polished single-piece replacement. Workers object that maintenance was the equipment’s advantage and its surviving irregularities explain more than an imagined pristine original.

Material inspection places limits on the object’s legend. Repairs, wear, and changes in custody can establish that it was used repeatedly without proving every story attached to it. Its value is relational: somebody can authenticate it, somebody needs it for an observance, and somebody may suffer if it is removed. An expensive replacement would not automatically inherit those relations. Custodians therefore record loans and repairs as carefully as ceremonial appearances. A collector who purchases the object but ignores its attached undertaking may own something that cannot safely be taken home.

entries.title: The Grove’s Empty Festival
entries.body:
One grove rests during the resin festival, displaying no trophies and hosting no procession. Visitors find it disappointing. Keepers point to recovering bark and nesting lizards, making absence itself the work that enables next year’s ordinary gathering.

The custom is learned through participation rather than a single authoritative text. Households disagree about details while recognizing enough shared actions to cooperate. That flexibility can admit newcomers or allow influential families to redefine the practice in their own favor. Describing it as ancient settles neither possibility. Its practical test is whether a participant can question a demand without losing access to food, water, or witnesses. Local reformers seek finite observances whose costs can be recorded, so that reverence for predecessors does not become an unanswerable demand upon children.

entries.title: The Herald’s Side of the Match
entries.body:
A training manuscript records the herald’s actions during every royal victory. It reveals that survival depended on trust and precise timing. Schools now use it to examine how a public story can conceal the cooperating person it casts as an enemy.

Copies disagree in ways that matter. A shortened phrase can remove a condition, and a copied date can imply that a later amendment belonged to the original undertaking. Dry writing preserves evidence but cannot make an oath binding by itself. Readers must distinguish a record of consent from a writer’s assertion that consent occurred. Marginal notes are sometimes the only surviving testimony of people excluded from the formal version. Establishing a trustworthy reading therefore depends on comparing custody, material, and ordinary expenses, as well as elegant arguments about wording.

entries.title: The Joined Shore Echo
entries.body:
A carved water trough repeats cheering sounds during high wind. Some interpret it as ancestors celebrating unity. Its sound ceased when a shelter was rebuilt nearby, provoking debate about whether restored ordinary welfare matters more than preserving the famous manifestation.

Witnesses distinguish an observed effect from their explanation for it. Repetition under comparable conditions is valuable evidence; a striking story told after its alleged cause becomes famous is weaker evidence. Masons, gardeners, and boat crews often recognize patterns an interpreter overlooks. Their explanation may reduce the immediate danger without settling whether an undertaking contributed to it. The basin has no institution capable of issuing a final answer for every manifestation. Communities record the conditions under which the effect occurs, then negotiate a response whose costs they can actually sustain.

entries.title: Coastal Resin Sealing
entries.body:
Seal workers apply resin in small heated batches, using scarce fuel and careful ventilation. Export promises leave local hulls waiting. Their seasonal agreements prioritize safe working boats, linking commercial freedom to duties the exclusive grant originally claimed to support.

The trade depends upon tools, training, reliable materials, and people who perform work its public account barely mentions. A skilled craftsperson can improve a process, yet every batch still requires hands and a season of available materials. Output remains bounded by fuel, animals, weather, and the hands available to repair equipment. Prices carry the history of these constraints into households far from the workshop. A commercial undertaking that survives its maker can preserve useful cooperation or prevent successors from adapting to changed conditions. The present negotiation concerns how to retain knowledge while releasing an obligation nobody can now perform.

entries.title: The Forest and the Fair
entries.body:
Forest workers propose financing independent fairs through a limited export levy. Circuit owners claim exclusive celebration rights. The dispute joins two inherited monopolies that once appeared unrelated but depended on the same households’ timber, labor, and access.

The dispute contains more than two positions. People with the same formal entitlement may face different practical costs, while opponents can depend upon the same canal, kitchen, or crossing. A complete settlement must describe an executable change rather than award a satisfying phrase to one side. Evidence about a past wrong remains necessary even when compensation cannot restore the original arrangement. Local negotiators separate immediate maintenance from the final assessment of responsibility. This allows a place to remain usable while its inhabitants continue an argument they have good reason not to abandon.
